decks.title: Indices (Exponents) — Part 1: The laws, zero, negative and fractional indices
goals: State and use the laws of indices for products, quotients, powers of powers, products and quotients in brackets
Explain why a zero index gives one and a negative index gives a reciprocal
Evaluate fractional indices as a root followed by a power

slides.heading: Indices (Exponents), Part 1
slides.body_md: A culture of one cell that doubles every hour has $2^{n}$ cells after $n$ hours. The index counts the doublings.

visual.alt: Table for a culture that starts with one cell and doubles every hour. After zero hours one cell, after one hour two, then four, eight, sixteen, thirty two and sixty four cells after six hours. Each cell count is two to the power of the number of hours.
visual.caption: The count after $n$ hours is $2^{n}$: the index counts the doublings.

slides.narration: Welcome to indices. A culture starts with one cell and doubles every hour. After three hours there are eight cells, and after six hours sixty four. The little number written above the base, the index, counts the doublings. In this part we learn the laws that let us calculate with indices, and what zero, negative and fractional indices mean.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
slides.narration: These are your goals for part one. First the five laws of indices. Then we ask what a zero index and a negative index can possibly mean, and the pattern will answer for us. Finally we meet fractional indices, which are roots in disguise, and we evaluate a number that has a negative fractional index.

slides.heading: What an index tells you
slides.body_md: In $a^{n}$, $a$ is the **base** and $n$ is the **index** (or exponent). The base is used as a factor $n$ times.

visual.alt: Table of six powers. Three to the fourth is three times three times three times three, eighty one. Two to the seventh is one hundred twenty eight. Five cubed is one hundred twenty five. Ten to the fifth is one hundred thousand. Minus two to the fifth is minus thirty two. One half to the fourth is one sixteenth.
visual.caption: In $a^{n}$, $a$ is the base and $n$ is the index (exponent): $a$ is used as a factor $n$ times.

slides.narration: Look at the table. Three to the fourth means three used as a factor four times, which is eighty one. Two to the seventh is one hundred twenty eight. A negative base works the same way: minus two to the fifth is minus thirty two. A fraction base is also fine, so one half to the fourth is one sixteenth.

slides.heading: Law 1: multiplying powers
slides.body_md: For the **same base**, add the indices: $a^{m} \times a^{n} = a^{m+n}$. Reason: $2^{3} \times 2^{4}$ is three twos times four twos, which is seven twos.

visual.alt: Table of four products of powers with the same base. Two cubed times two to the fourth is two to the seventh, one hundred twenty eight. Three squared times three to the fifth is three to the seventh, two thousand one hundred eighty seven. Five times five cubed is five to the fourth, six hundred twenty five. Ten squared times ten to the fourth is one million.
visual.caption: Same base: $a^{m} \times a^{n} = a^{m+n}$.

slides.narration: To multiply powers of the same base, add the indices. Two cubed times two to the fourth is three twos times four twos, so seven twos: one hundred twenty eight. The rule needs the same base. Never multiply the bases, and never add the indices when the bases are different.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: products and quotients
slides.body_md: Simplify $\dfrac{5^{8} \times 5^{6}}{5^{11}}$ and find its value.

rows: Add the indices in the product
Subtract the index in the quotient

visual.alt: Table of three steps for five to the eighth times five to the sixth over five to the eleventh. Add the indices in the product to get five to the fourteenth; subtract eleven to get five cubed; the value is one hundred twenty five.
visual.caption: Add in the product, subtract in the quotient, then evaluate.

slides.narration: First the product on top: five to the eighth times five to the sixth is five to the fourteenth, because eight plus six is fourteen. Then divide by five to the eleventh, which subtracts eleven from fourteen and leaves five cubed. Five cubed is one hundred twenty five.

slides.heading: Law 2: dividing powers
slides.body_md: For the **same base**, subtract the indices: $a^{m} \div a^{n} = a^{m-n}$. When $m = n$ the answer is $a^{0}$, which is $1$.

visual.alt: Table of four quotients of powers with the same base. Two to the ninth divided by two to the fourth is two to the fifth, thirty two. Three to the eighth over three to the fifth is twenty seven. Seven to the sixth over seven to the sixth is seven to the zero, one. Ten to the seventh over ten cubed is ten thousand.
visual.caption: Same base: $a^{m} \div a^{n} = a^{m-n}$ (and when $m = n$ the result is $a^{0} = 1$).

slides.narration: To divide powers of the same base, subtract the indices. Two to the ninth divided by two to the fourth is two to the fifth, thirty two. Look at the third row: seven to the sixth divided by seven to the sixth is seven to the zero. But a number divided by itself is one, and that already hints at what a zero index means.

slides.heading: Quick check: a wrong power law
slides.narration: Decide whether the indices should be added or multiplied when a power is raised to a power. Then work out both sides.

slides.heading: Laws 3, 4 and 5: brackets
slides.body_md: $(a^{m})^{n} = a^{mn}$, $(ab)^{n} = a^{n}b^{n}$ and $\left(\dfrac{a}{b}\right)^{n} = \dfrac{a^{n}}{b^{n}}$.

visual.alt: Table of three laws. A power of a power multiplies the indices: two cubed to the fourth is two to the twelfth, four thousand ninety six, and three squared cubed is three to the sixth, seven hundred twenty nine. A power of a product goes to each factor: two times five, cubed, is one thousand. A power of a quotient goes to top and bottom: two thirds to the fourth is sixteen eighty firsts.
visual.caption: Powers distribute over products and quotients, and multiply across brackets.

slides.narration: Three more laws deal with brackets. A power of a power multiplies the indices, so two cubed, to the fourth, is two to the twelfth. A power of a product goes to each factor: two times five, cubed, is two cubed times five cubed, which is one thousand. And a power of a quotient goes to the top and the bottom.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: all three at once

rows: Multiply the indices in the bracket
Add the indices in the product
Subtract the index in the quotient

visual.alt: Table of three steps for twelve cubed squared times twelve to the fourth over twelve to the eighth. The bracket gives twelve to the sixth; the product gives twelve to the tenth; the quotient gives twelve squared, one hundred forty four.
visual.caption: Three laws in one line: bracket, product, quotient.

slides.narration: Work in layers. The bracket multiplies the indices: three times two is six. The product adds: six plus four is ten. The quotient subtracts: ten minus eight is two. So the answer is twelve squared, one hundred forty four. A calculator would struggle with twelve to the tenth, but the laws make it easy.

slides.heading: The zero index
slides.body_md: Keep dividing by $3$: each step lowers the index by $1$. The pattern reaches $3^{0} = 1$. In general $a^{0} = 1$ for $a \ne 0$.

visual.alt: Table showing the pattern three to the fourth is eighty one, three cubed is twenty seven, three squared is nine, three to the first is three, and three to the zero is one. Each line is the line above divided by three, so the zero index gives one.
visual.caption: Dividing by $3$ each time lowers the index by $1$, and $3^{0} = 1$.

slides.narration: Here is a pattern. Three to the fourth is eighty one. Divide by three to get three cubed, twenty seven, then nine, then three. Divide three by three once more and we reach one, and the index has dropped to zero. So three to the zero is one. The same works for every base except zero, so any non-zero number to the zero is one.

slides.heading: Quick check: is seven to the zero zero?
slides.body_md: Jaya says $7^{0} = 0$.
slides.narration: Use the quotient law on seven cubed divided by seven cubed, and also say what a number divided by itself equals.

slides.heading: Negative indices
slides.body_md: Keep going below zero: $2^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{2}$, $2^{-2} = \dfrac{1}{4}$. A negative index gives the **reciprocal**: $a^{-n} = \dfrac{1}{a^{n}}$.

visual.alt: Table of powers of two from two cubed down to two to the minus three: eight, four, two, one, one half, one quarter, one eighth. A negative index gives the reciprocal: two to the minus three is one over two cubed.
visual.caption: A negative index means the reciprocal: $a^{-n} = \dfrac{1}{a^{n}}$.

slides.narration: Continue the halving pattern below zero. Two to the zero is one, two to the minus one is one half, two to the minus two is one quarter, and two to the minus three is one eighth. A negative index does not make the number negative. It gives the reciprocal: two to the minus three is one over two cubed.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: negative indices
slides.body_md: Evaluate $\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^{-4} + 4^{-2} \times 2^{5}$.

visual.alt: Table of three steps for two thirds to the minus four plus four to the minus two times two to the fifth. The first term is eighty one sixteenths. The second is two. The sum is one hundred thirteen sixteenths.
visual.caption: A negative index flips the base; bring different bases to a common base before adding indices.

slides.narration: For the first term, a negative index flips the fraction, so two thirds to the minus four is three halves to the fourth, eighty one sixteenths. For the second term, write four as two squared so that the bases match: two to the minus four times two to the fifth is two to the first, which is two. Then add: eighty one sixteenths and two make one hundred thirteen sixteenths.

slides.heading: Quick check: adding negative powers
slides.body_md: Do not add the indices when the powers are added.
slides.narration: Write each power as a fraction of a metre first, using the reciprocal. Then add the two fractions with a common denominator.

slides.heading: Fractional indices: roots
slides.body_md: $a^{\frac{1}{q}}$ is the $q$th root of $a$: the number whose $q$th power is $a$. For example $64^{\frac{1}{3}} = 4$ because $4^{3} = 64$.

visual.alt: Table of six fractional indices. Sixty four to the one third is the cube root, four, since four cubed is sixty four. Eighty one to the one quarter is three. Thirty two to the one fifth is two. Forty nine to the one half is seven. One thousand to the one third is ten. Six hundred twenty five to the one quarter is five.
visual.caption: $a^{\frac{1}{q}}$ is the $q$th root of $a$: the number whose $q$th power is $a$.

slides.narration: A fractional index with a one on top is a root. Sixty four to the one third is the cube root of sixty four, which is four, because four cubed is sixty four. Eighty one to the one quarter is three. Thirty two to the one fifth is two. The check column shows each root raised to its own power to get back the original number.

slides.heading: The index p over q: root and power
slides.body_md: $a^{\frac{p}{q}} = \left(\sqrt[q]{a}\right)^{p}$. The **denominator** is the root, the **numerator** is the power. Take the root first.

headers: Write $a$ as a power of the root

visual.alt: Table of five powers with fractional indices. Two hundred forty three to the three fifths is three cubed, twenty seven. One hundred twenty eight to the five sevenths is two to the fifth, thirty two. Three hundred forty three to the two thirds is forty nine. Six hundred twenty five to the three quarters is one hundred twenty five. Thirty six to the three halves is two hundred sixteen.
visual.caption: $a^{\frac{p}{q}} = \left(\sqrt[q]{a}\right)^{p}$: take the root first, then the power.

slides.narration: In an index like three fifths, the denominator tells you the root and the numerator tells you the power. For two hundred forty three to the three fifths, take the fifth root, which is three, and then cube it to get twenty seven. Taking the root first keeps the numbers small. Be careful not to swap the numerator and denominator.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a negative fractional index
slides.body_md: Evaluate $\left(\dfrac{27}{64}\right)^{-\frac{2}{3}}$.

rows: Flip the fraction to remove the minus sign
Cube root of top and bottom

visual.alt: Table of three steps for twenty seven sixty fourths to the minus two thirds. Flip to sixty four twenty sevenths to the two thirds. The cube root is four thirds. Squaring gives sixteen ninths.
visual.caption: Order: reciprocal, root, power.

slides.narration: Three jobs, in order. The minus sign flips the fraction, giving sixty four twenty sevenths. The denominator three means a cube root: the cube root of sixty four is four and of twenty seven is three, so four thirds. The numerator two means square it. The answer is sixteen ninths.

slides.heading: Quick check: the error in a fractional index
slides.body_md: Amit calculates $64^{\frac{2}{3}}$ as $\dfrac{64^{2}}{3}$.
slides.narration: Remember which of the two numbers in the index is the root. Then work out the correct value and compare it with his answer.

slides.heading: One curve for every index
slides.body_md: The graph of $y = 2^{x}$ passes through $(0, 1)$, doubles with each step to the right and shrinks towards the axis on the left, but is **never zero or negative**.

visual.alt: Graph of y equals two to the x for x from minus three to four. The curve is always above the x axis, passes through zero one, and doubles for every step to the right. Marked points: minus two, one quarter; minus one, one half; zero, one; one, two; two, four; three, eight. For negative x it gets close to the axis without reaching it.
visual.caption: Positive for every $x$; $2^{0} = 1$ and $2^{-n} = \dfrac{1}{2^{n}}$ are small but never $0$.

slides.narration: Here is the graph of two to the x. At zero it is one. Each step to the right doubles the height. Each step to the left halves it, so two to the minus two is one quarter. The curve gets very close to the axis on the left but never touches it, which is why a power of two can never be zero or negative.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Same base: add indices to multiply, subtract to divide
$(a^{m})^{n} = a^{mn}$; powers go to each factor of a product or quotient
$a^{\frac{p}{q}}$: take the $q$th root, then the $p$th power

rows: Product and quotient in a bracket

visual.alt: Summary table for part one. Product law adds indices, quotient law subtracts them, power of a power multiplies them, a power of a product or quotient goes to each factor, a zero index gives one, a negative index gives the reciprocal, and a fractional index is a root and a power.
visual.caption: Part 1 on one card (for $a, b > 0$ with fractional indices).

slides.narration: To sum up part one. For the same base, add indices to multiply and subtract them to divide. A power of a power multiplies the indices, and a power of a product or quotient goes to each factor. A zero index gives one, a negative index gives the reciprocal, and a fractional index is a root followed by a power. Next we use these ideas to simplify and to solve equations.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Evaluate a number with a fractional index (2 to 3 marks):** reciprocal for a negative sign 1 + root 1 + power and answer 1
**Simplify with several laws (3 marks):** each law applied correctly 1 + final single power 1 + value 1
**Mistake:** adding the indices of a power of a power
**Mistake:** believing that $a^{0} = 0$ or that $a^{-n}$ is negative
slides.narration: In a calculation, always show the law you are using. Add indices for products, subtract for quotients, multiply for brackets. Take roots first, so the numbers stay small. Remember that a zero index gives one, and a negative index gives a reciprocal, not a negative number. And do not swap the root and the power in a fractional index.

decks.title: Indices (Exponents) — Part 2: Simplifying and solving exponential equations
goals: Reduce a numerical expression with several bases to one base and simplify it
Simplify algebraic expressions with several letters and indices
Simplify expressions with an unknown in the index by factoring the smallest power
Solve exponential equations by equating indices, including sums of powers

slides.heading: Indices (Exponents), Part 2
slides.body_md: One idea solves most index problems: write everything with the **same base**, apply the laws, and then equate the indices.

nodes.label: Write each base as a power of a small prime or a common base
Use the laws: add, subtract or multiply indices
Equation: the bases are equal, so equate the indices
Solve for $x$ and check by substitution

visual.alt: Flow chart of the common base strategy: look at the bases, write each as a power of a small prime or a common base, use the laws of indices, simplify to a single power, for an equation equate the indices, then solve for x and check by substitution.
visual.caption: One idea, five steps: common base, laws, single power, equate, check.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. Almost every index problem has the same plan. Look at the bases. Write each as a power of a small number, so that the bases match. Use the laws to reach a single power. If it is an equation, equate the indices, solve, and finally check by substituting.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Bring different bases to a **common base**
Solve **exponential equations** and check the answer
slides.narration: These are your goals for part two. We start with numbers, then letters, then expressions where the index itself contains an unknown. After that come exponential equations, including those with a sum of powers, and we finish by noticing the equations that have no solution at all.

slides.heading: Common base: prime powers
slides.body_md: Write numbers as **prime powers** so that the laws can be used. For $72$: $72 = 2^{3} \times 3^{2}$.

visual.alt: Table of five numbers as prime powers. Seventy two is two cubed times three squared. One hundred eight is two squared times three cubed. One hundred forty four is two to the fourth times three squared. Two hundred sixteen is two cubed times three cubed. One thousand two hundred ninety six is two to the fourth times three to the fourth.
visual.caption: Prime powers make every law of indices usable.

slides.narration: The laws work only for the same base, so factorise first. Seventy two is two cubed times three squared. One hundred forty four is two to the fourth times three squared. And one thousand two hundred ninety six is two to the fourth times three to the fourth, which is six to the fourth. Prime powers are the safest common language.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: fractional indices together
slides.body_md: Evaluate $\dfrac{32^{\frac{2}{5}} \times 27^{\frac{1}{3}}}{81^{\frac{3}{4}}}$.

visual.alt: Table of two steps for thirty two to the two fifths times twenty seven to the one third over eighty one to the three quarters. The roots give four, three and twenty seven. The result is twelve over twenty seven, four ninths.
visual.caption: Take every root exactly, then multiply and divide the whole numbers.

slides.narration: Take each root exactly. Thirty two is two to the fifth, so its two fifths power is two squared, four. Twenty seven to the one third is three. Eighty one is three to the fourth, so its three quarters power is three cubed, twenty seven. The fraction is twelve over twenty seven, and dividing top and bottom by three gives four ninths.

slides.heading: Indices with letters
slides.body_md: Treat each letter separately: **add** the indices of a letter in a product, **subtract** in a quotient and **multiply** for a bracket.

visual.alt: Table of four algebraic expressions. x to the fourth y to the minus two times x to the minus one y to the fifth gives x cubed y cubed. a cubed b to the minus four over a to the minus two b to the minus one gives a to the fifth b to the minus three. p squared q to the minus three, cubed, gives p to the sixth q to the minus nine. m to the minus two over n cubed, to the minus two, gives m to the fourth n to the sixth.
visual.caption: Treat each letter separately: add, subtract or multiply its indices.

slides.narration: With letters, handle each letter on its own. In the first row, x has indices four and minus one, which add to three. The letter y has minus two and five, which add to three. In the second row, subtract: three minus minus two is five. In the bracket rows, multiply every index by the outer index.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a long expression
slides.body_md: Simplify $\dfrac{(x^{2}y^{-3})^{-2}(x^{-1}y^{4})^{3}}{x^{-5}y^{2}}$ with positive indices.

visual.alt: Table of five steps. The first bracket gives x to the minus four y to the sixth. The second gives x to the minus three y to the twelfth. The numerator is x to the minus seven y to the eighteenth. Dividing by x to the minus five y squared gives x to the minus two y to the sixteenth, which is y to the sixteenth over x squared.
visual.caption: Letter by letter: $x$: $-4 - 3 + 5 = -2$; $y$: $6 + 12 - 2 = 16$.

slides.narration: Open each bracket by multiplying its indices. The first gives x to the minus four and y to the sixth. The second gives x to the minus three and y to the twelfth. Multiply them and add the indices: x to the minus seven, y to the eighteenth. Now divide by x to the minus five and y squared by subtracting. For x, minus seven minus minus five is minus two. For y, eighteen minus two is sixteen.

slides.heading: Quick check: a machine formula
slides.body_md: Work letter by letter.
slides.narration: Open the bracket first by multiplying each index by two. Then divide by subtracting the indices of each letter, and take care with the minus signs.

slides.heading: An unknown in the index
slides.body_md: Use $a^{n+k} = a^{n} \times a^{k}$ to split the power, then **factor out the smallest power**. The result often does not depend on $n$.

visual.alt: Table for n from zero to four of six to the n plus two minus six to the n over six to the n plus one. The top is thirty five, two hundred ten, one thousand two hundred sixty and so on, the bottom is six, thirty six, two hundred sixteen and so on, and the ratio is always thirty five sixths.
visual.caption: The ratio does not depend on $n$: $\dfrac{6^{n}(36 - 1)}{6^{n} \times 6} = \dfrac{35}{6}$.

slides.narration: When the index contains an unknown, split it with the product law. Six to the n plus two is six to the n times thirty six. So the top of the fraction is six to the n times thirty five. The bottom is six to the n times six. The six to the n cancels, and the ratio is thirty five sixths for every n. The table confirms it for n from zero to four.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: factor the smallest power
slides.body_md: Simplify $\dfrac{2^{n+3} + 2^{n+1}}{5 \times 2^{n}}$.

visual.alt: Table of two steps for two to the n plus three plus two to the n plus one, over five times two to the n. The numerator is ten times two to the n. Dividing by five times two to the n leaves two, for every n.
visual.caption: Spot the smallest power, factor it out, and cancel.

slides.narration: Split each power: two to the n plus three is eight times two to the n, and two to the n plus one is two times two to the n. Factor out two to the n: it is multiplied by eight plus two, which is ten. Now divide by five times two to the n. The two to the n cancels, leaving ten over five, which is two. The answer is two for every n.

slides.heading: Quick check: rewrite a power with an unknown
slides.body_md: Which expression equals $2^{n+3}$?
slides.narration: Use the product law backwards to split the index. Then test your choice with a small value of n, such as two.

slides.heading: Exponential equations: equate the indices
slides.body_md: If $a > 0$ and $a \ne 1$, then $a^{m} = a^{n}$ means $m = n$. So write both sides as powers of the **same base**.

visual.alt: Table of four equations. Three to the x equals eighty one becomes three to the fourth, so x is four. Three to the x equals one twenty seventh becomes three to the minus three, so x is minus three. Three to the x minus one equals nine gives x minus one equals two, x is three. Two to the two x equals thirty two gives two x equals five, x is five halves.
visual.caption: If $a > 0$ and $a \ne 1$, then $a^{m} = a^{n}$ means $m = n$.

slides.narration: An exponential equation has the unknown in the index. If both sides are powers of the same base, which is positive and not one, then the indices must be equal. Three to the x equals eighty one becomes three to the x equals three to the fourth, so x is four. For a fraction on the right, a negative index appears, as in the second row.

slides.heading: Reading it on a graph
slides.body_md: Solving $2^{x} = 16$ means asking where the curve $y = 2^{x}$ meets the line $y = 16$. It is rising, so there is **exactly one** solution.

visual.alt: Graph of y equals two to the x and the horizontal line y equals sixteen for x from zero to six. The curve rises steadily and meets the line at exactly one point, x equal to four, y equal to sixteen. So two to the x equals sixteen has exactly one solution.
visual.caption: The curve $y = 2^{x}$ is always rising, so it meets $y = 16$ once: $2^{x} = 16$ gives $x = 4$.

slides.narration: Here is the same idea on a graph. The curve of two to the x keeps rising. The horizontal line at sixteen cuts it once, at x equal to four. A rising curve can meet a horizontal line at most once, which is why an exponential equation of this kind has at most one solution. Equating indices finds it exactly.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a fractional answer

visual.alt: Table of four steps for four to the x plus one equals five hundred twelve. Write four as two squared and five hundred twelve as two to the ninth. Equate the indices: two x plus two equals nine. So x is seven halves. Check: four to the nine halves is two to the ninth, five hundred twelve.
visual.caption: The answer need not be a whole number.

slides.narration: Write four as two squared, so four to the x plus one is two to the two x plus two. Five hundred twelve is two to the ninth. Now equate the indices: two x plus two equals nine, so two x is seven and x is seven halves. A solution does not have to be a whole number. To check, four to the nine halves is two to the ninth, which is five hundred twelve.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a sum of powers

visual.alt: Table of four steps for seven to the x plus seven to the x plus one equals three hundred ninety two. Factor out seven to the x to get eight times seven to the x. Divide by eight: seven to the x is forty nine, seven squared. So x is two. Check: forty nine plus three hundred forty three is three hundred ninety two.
visual.caption: Do not equate indices until there is a single power on each side.

slides.narration: Here the left side is a sum, so you cannot equate indices yet. Split seven to the x plus one as seven times seven to the x, and factor out seven to the x. We get eight times seven to the x. Divide three hundred ninety two by eight to get forty nine, which is seven squared. So x is two. Check: forty nine plus three hundred forty three is three hundred ninety two.

slides.heading: Quick check: two bases
slides.body_md: Bring both bases to base $3$.
slides.narration: Write nine as three squared, and the right side as a power of three. Then add the indices on the left and equate.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: different bases

visual.alt: Table of four steps for twenty five to the x plus one equals one hundred twenty five to the x minus one. Write both as powers of five. Equate: two x plus two equals three x minus three. So x is five. Check: twenty five to the sixth and one hundred twenty five to the fourth are both five to the twelfth.
visual.caption: Different bases that are powers of the same number need one common base.

slides.narration: Twenty five and one hundred twenty five are both powers of five. So the left side is five to the two times x plus one, and the right side is five to the three times x minus one. Be careful to multiply the whole bracket. Equate the indices: two x plus two equals three x minus three, so x is five. Both sides come to five to the twelfth.

slides.heading: When there is no solution
slides.body_md: For $a > 0$, $a^{x}$ is **always positive**. So $2^{x} = -4$ and $5^{x} = 0$ have no solution, and the rule fails for the base $1$.

rows: a positive base raised to any power is positive
a power of a positive base is never $0$
$1$ raised to any power is $1$, so the equation is always true
a fraction needs a negative index: $\dfrac{1}{9} = 3^{-2}$

visual.alt: Table of five equations. Two to the x equals minus four has no solution. Five to the x equals zero has no solution. One to the x equals one is true for every x. One to the x equals five has no solution. Three to the x equals one ninth has the solution x equals minus two.
visual.caption: Check the base first: for $a > 0$, $a^{x}$ is always positive, and the rule needs $a \ne 1$.

slides.narration: Sometimes there is no solution. A positive base raised to any power is positive, so two to the x can never be minus four, and five to the x is never zero. The base one is special: one to any power is one, so one to the x equals one is true for every x, and one to the x equals five is never true. Always look at the base first.

slides.heading: Quick check: which has no solution?
slides.body_md: Look at the sign of the right side.
slides.narration: For each equation, ask whether a positive base to some power can equal the number on the right. Only one of them is impossible.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: one value, three bases

sections.heading: 1. Index form and the laws of indices
sections.body_md:
In $a^{n}$, $a$ is the **base** and $n$ the **index** (exponent): $a$ is used as a factor $n$ times, so $2^{7} = 128$.

For the **same base** $a > 0$:
- $a^{m} \times a^{n} = a^{m+n}$ and $a^{m} \div a^{n} = a^{m-n}$.
- $(a^{m})^{n} = a^{mn}$.
- $(ab)^{n} = a^{n}b^{n}$ and $\left(\dfrac{a}{b}\right)^{n} = \dfrac{a^{n}}{b^{n}}$.

The laws need the same base: $2^{3} \times 3^{4}$ cannot be combined, and $2^{3} \times 2^{4} = 2^{7}$, not $4^{7}$.

key_terms.definition_md: The number that is multiplied by itself in a power, such as $2$ in $2^{7}$.
The number of times the base is used as a factor, written above the base.

Ten squared times ten to the fourth is one million.

sections.heading: 2. Zero and negative indices
sections.body_md:
Divide $3^{4}$ by $3$ repeatedly: $81, 27, 9, 3, 1, \dfrac{1}{3}, \dfrac{1}{9}$. The index drops by $1$ each time, so $3^{0} = 1$, $3^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{3}$ and $3^{-2} = \dfrac{1}{9}$. The quotient law agrees: $a^{3} \div a^{3} = a^{0}$ and the quotient is $1$.

- $a^{0} = 1$ for every $a \ne 0$.
- $a^{-n} = \dfrac{1}{a^{n}}$, and $\left(\dfrac{a}{b}\right)^{-n} = \left(\dfrac{b}{a}\right)^{n}$.
- A negative index gives a reciprocal; the number stays positive when the base is positive.

visual.alt: Table showing the pattern three to the fourth is eighty one, three cubed is twenty seven, three squared is nine, three to the first is three, and three to the zero is one. Each line is the line above divided by three, so the zero index gives one.
visual.caption: Dividing by $3$ each time lowers the index by $1$, and $3^{0} = 1$.

sections.heading: 3. Fractional indices
sections.body_md:
$a^{\frac{1}{q}}$ is the $q$th root of $a$ (for $a > 0$): $64^{\frac{1}{3}} = 4$ because $4^{3} = 64$.

$a^{\frac{p}{q}} = \left(\sqrt[q]{a}\right)^{p}$: the **denominator** is the root and the **numerator** is the power. Take the root first: $243^{\frac{3}{5}} = 3^{3} = 27$.

The laws of indices also hold for fractional indices, for example $a^{\frac{1}{2}} \times a^{\frac{1}{2}} = a$.

key_terms.definition_md: $a^{\frac{p}{q}}$ means the $q$th root of $a$ raised to the power $p$.
The $q$th root of $a$ is the number whose $q$th power is $a$.

sections.heading: 5. Simplifying with a common base and with letters
sections.body_md:
Write numbers as prime powers so that the bases match: $72 = 2^{3} \times 3^{2}$, $1296 = 2^{4} \times 3^{4}$. Then use the laws.

With letters, treat each letter separately: $\dfrac{(x^{2}y^{-3})^{-2}(x^{-1}y^{4})^{3}}{x^{-5}y^{2}} = x^{-2}y^{16} = \dfrac{y^{16}}{x^{2}}$ (for $x$: $-4 - 3 + 5 = -2$; for $y$: $6 + 12 - 2 = 16$).

Give the final answer with positive indices when asked, and remember $x^{0} = 1$.

key_terms.definition_md: A power of a prime number, such as $2^{4}$ or $3^{2}$.

sections.heading: 6. Expressions with an unknown in the index
sections.body_md:
Split a power with $a^{n+k} = a^{n} \times a^{k}$, then **factor out the smallest power**.

$\dfrac{2^{n+3} + 2^{n+1}}{5 \times 2^{n}} = \dfrac{2^{n}(8 + 2)}{5 \times 2^{n}} = 2$, and $\dfrac{6^{n+2} - 6^{n}}{6^{n+1}} = \dfrac{35}{6}$ for every $n$.

A result that does not contain $n$ is the same for all $n$: test it with a few values.

key_terms.definition_md: The smallest power, such as $2^{n}$, that divides every term.

The top is thirty five, two hundred ten, one thousand two hundred sixty and so on, the bottom is six, thirty six, two hundred sixteen and so on, and the ratio is always thirty five sixths.
visual.caption: The ratio does not depend on $n$: $\dfrac{6^{n}(36 - 1)}{6^{n} \times 6} = \dfrac{35}{6}$.

sections.heading: 7. Exponential equations
sections.body_md:
For $a > 0$ and $a \ne 1$: $a^{m} = a^{n}$ means $m = n$. Write both sides as powers of the same base, equate the indices, solve, and **check by substitution**.

- $4^{x+1} = 512$: $2^{2x+2} = 2^{9}$, so $x = \dfrac{7}{2}$.
- $25^{x+1} = 125^{x-1}$: $2x + 2 = 3x - 3$, so $x = 5$.
- A sum of powers: $7^{x} + 7^{x+1} = 8 \times 7^{x} = 392$, so $7^{x} = 49$ and $x = 2$.
- If $2^{20} = 4^{y} = 32^{z}$, write each base as a power of $2$: $y = 10$ and $z = 4$.

A positive base never gives a negative number or zero: $2^{x} = -4$ has no solution. For the base $1$ the rule fails.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *Evaluate a number with a fractional index (2 to 3 marks):* reciprocal for a negative sign 1; root 1; power and value 1.
- *Simplify with several laws (3 marks):* each law applied correctly 1; a single power 1; value 1.
- *Algebraic simplification (3 marks):* brackets opened 1; indices of each letter combined 1; positive-index form 1.
- *Solve an exponential equation (2 to 3 marks):* common base 1; indices equated 1; value with a check 1.
- *Sum of powers (3 marks):* smallest power factored out 1; a single power 1; $x$ found 1.
- *10-mark structured question:* parts (a), (b), (c) usually 3 + 3 + 4; show every law you use.

**Common mistakes**
1. Multiplying the bases: $2^{3} \times 2^{4} = 4^{7}$ is wrong; the base stays and the indices add.
2. Adding the indices of a power of a power: $(5^{2})^{3} = 5^{6}$, not $5^{5}$.
3. Believing that $a^{0} = 0$, or that $a^{-n}$ is a negative number.
4. Swapping root and power in $a^{\frac{p}{q}}$, or using a calculator before taking an exact root.
5. Equating indices when the bases are different, or adding the indices in $2^{x} + 2^{x+1}$.
6. Not multiplying the whole bracket, as in $27^{x-1} = 3^{3x-3}$, not $3^{3x-1}$.
7. Missing a case with no solution: $2^{x} = -4$ and $5^{x} = 0$.

cards.front_md: What are the **base** and the **index** in $a^{n}$?
cards.back_md: The base $a$ is the number used as a factor; the index $n$ says how many times. $2^{7} = 128$.
An equation with the unknown in an index, such as $2^{x+1} = 32$.
$a^{\frac{p}{q}}$ is the $q$th root of $a$ raised to the power $p$, for $a > 0$.
It gives the reciprocal: $a^{-n} = \dfrac{1}{a^{n}}$.
A power of a prime, such as $2^{4}$ or $3^{2}$. Numbers written as prime powers can be combined with the laws.

cards.front_md: Power of a product and of a quotient?
cards.back_md: $(ab)^{n} = a^{n}b^{n}$ and $\left(\dfrac{a}{b}\right)^{n} = \dfrac{a^{n}}{b^{n}}$.
$a^{0} = 1$ for every $a \ne 0$ (from $a^{m} \div a^{m} = a^{0}$).
$\left(\sqrt[q]{a}\right)^{p}$: denominator is the root, numerator is the power.

cards.front_md: Why can the laws of indices not combine $2^{3} \times 3^{4}$?
cards.back_md: The bases are different. The laws need the same base; otherwise evaluate or write both as powers of one base.
Dividing $a^{3}$ by $a^{3}$ gives $a^{3-3} = a^{0}$, but any non-zero number divided by itself is $1$.
Not because of the sign of the index: $2^{-3} = \dfrac{1}{8}$ is positive. It is a reciprocal.

cards.front_md: In what order do you evaluate $\left(\dfrac{27}{64}\right)^{-\frac{2}{3}}$?
cards.back_md: Flip for the minus sign, take the cube root, then square: $\left(\dfrac{64}{27}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}} = \left(\dfrac{4}{3}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{16}{9}$.

cards.front_md: When can you equate the indices of $a^{m} = a^{n}$?
cards.back_md: When both sides are single powers of the same base with $a > 0$ and $a \ne 1$.
Factor the smallest power: $2^{x}(8 + 1) = 9 \times 2^{x}$.
No. A positive base to any power is positive, so $2^{x} = -4$ and $2^{x} = 0$ have no solution.
The fourth root is $2$ and $2^{3} = 8$, so $8$.
Flip to $\left(\dfrac{25}{9}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}} = \dfrac{5}{3}$.
Multiplying the bases to get $4^{7}$. The base stays: $2^{7} = 128$.
Adding the indices to get $5^{5}$. Multiply: $5^{6} = 15625$.

cards.front_md: Before checking a solution of $7^{x} + 7^{x+1} = 392$, what is the key step?
cards.back_md: Factor out $7^{x}$: $8 \times 7^{x} = 392$, so $7^{x} = 49$. Never equate indices of a sum.

cards.front_md: Picture: the graph of $y = 2^{x}$. What do you see at $x = 0$ and as $x$ becomes very negative?
cards.back_md: It passes through $(0, 1)$ and gets close to the axis without reaching it: $2^{-n} = \dfrac{1}{2^{n}}$ is small but positive.

cards.front_md: Picture: the curve $y = 2^{x}$ and the line $y = 16$. How many solutions does $2^{x} = 16$ have?
cards.back_md: One, at $x = 4$: a rising curve meets a horizontal line at most once.

questions.stem_md: Which expression is equal to $a^{m} \times a^{n}$, for a positive number $a$ and whole numbers $m$ and $n$?
questions.solution_md: The product law says that powers of the same base are multiplied by adding the indices: $a^{m} \times a^{n} = a^{m+n}$. For example $2^{3} \times 2^{4} = 2^{7} = 128$, but $2^{12}$ (the product of the indices) is $4096$.

questions.stem_md: A petri dish starts with $4^{3}$ cells. After a nutrient dose the count is multiplied by $4^{5}$. The new count is $4^{k}$ cells, where $k$ equals
questions.solution_md: The cells are multiplied, and the base $4$ is the same, so the indices add: $4^{3} \times 4^{5} = 4^{3+5} = 4^{8}$ and $k = 8$. The value $15$ comes from multiplying the indices.

questions.stem_md: Tanvi's memory card holds $2^{35}$ bytes. One video clip needs $2^{27}$ bytes. The number of such clips that fill the card exactly is
questions.solution_md: The number of clips is $2^{35} \div 2^{27}$. Dividing powers of the same base subtracts the indices: $2^{35-27} = 2^{8} = 256$ clips. Adding the indices would give $2^{62}$, which is the product of the two sizes, not their quotient.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is equal to $(5^{2})^{6}$?
questions.solution_md: The power of a power law multiplies the indices: $(5^{2})^{6} = 5^{2 \times 6} = 5^{12}$. Adding gives $5^{8}$, the usual slip. Also $25^{8} = 5^{16}$, which is a different number.

questions.stem_md: A square courtyard has side $2^{3} \times 5^{2}$ metres. Its area, in square metres, written with prime bases, is
questions.solution_md: Area $= (2^{3} \times 5^{2})^{2}$. A power of a product is the product of the powers, and a power of a power multiplies the indices: $2^{3 \times 2} \times 5^{2 \times 2} = 2^{6} \times 5^{4}$, which is $64 \times 625 = 40000$ m$^2$.

questions.stem_md: Jaya says that $7^{0} = 0$, because "no sevens are being multiplied". The correct value of $7^{0}$ is
questions.solution_md: By the quotient law, $7^{3} \div 7^{3} = 7^{3-3} = 7^{0}$. But any non-zero number divided by itself is $1$, so $7^{0} = 1$. The same pattern holds for every non-zero base.

questions.stem_md: A photocopier setting enlarges by the factor $\left(\dfrac{3}{7}\right)^{-2}$. This factor is equal to
questions.solution_md: A negative index takes the reciprocal of the base: $\left(\dfrac{3}{7}\right)^{-2} = \left(\dfrac{7}{3}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{49}{9}$. The factor is positive and larger than $1$, so it is an enlargement; the index $-2$ does not make the number negative.

questions.stem_md: Vihaan adds two lengths, $5^{-1}$ m and $5^{-2}$ m. The total length, in metres, is
questions.solution_md: $5^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{5} = \dfrac{5}{25}$ and $5^{-2} = \dfrac{1}{25}$, so the sum is $\dfrac{6}{25}$ m. The index law $a^{m} \times a^{n} = a^{m+n}$ is for products; adding the indices to get $5^{-3} = \dfrac{1}{125}$ is a slip.

questions.stem_md: A cubical tank holds $343$ m$^3$ of water. The area of one square face, in square metres, is $343^{\frac{2}{3}}$, which equals
questions.solution_md: The denominator $3$ means a cube root: $343^{\frac{1}{3}} = 7$, because $7^{3} = 343$. The numerator $2$ is the power: $343^{\frac{2}{3}} = 7^{2} = 49$. So each face has area $49$ m$^2$.

questions.stem_md: A scale model of a bearing is built with the ratio $\left(\dfrac{16}{81}\right)^{-\frac{3}{4}}$. The value of this ratio is
questions.solution_md: Flip the fraction to remove the minus sign: $\left(\dfrac{81}{16}\right)^{\frac{3}{4}}$. The fourth root of $\dfrac{81}{16}$ is $\dfrac{3}{2}$, and cubing it gives $\dfrac{27}{8}$.

questions.stem_md: A square mat has side $\sqrt[5]{243^{2}}$ units. The side of the mat is
questions.solution_md: $\sqrt[5]{243^{2}} = 243^{\frac{2}{5}}$. Since $243 = 3^{5}$, the fifth root is $3$, and $3^{2} = 9$. The side is $9$ units.

questions.stem_md: Amit evaluates $64^{\frac{2}{3}}$ as $\dfrac{64^{2}}{3}$ and gets $\dfrac{4096}{3}$. Which statement about his work is correct?

options.text_md: He is wrong: the correct value is $64^{2} \times 3 = 12288$.
He is wrong: the numerator $2$ is the root, so the value is $\sqrt{64^{3}} = 512$.
He is right: a fractional index means "raise to the power, then divide by the denominator".
He is wrong: the denominator $3$ means a cube root, so $64^{\frac{2}{3}} = \left(\sqrt[3]{64}\right)^{2} = 16$.

questions.solution_md: In $a^{\frac{p}{q}}$ the denominator $q$ is the root and the numerator $p$ is the power. So $64^{\frac{2}{3}} = (\sqrt[3]{64})^{2} = 4^{2} = 16$. Amit's $\dfrac{4096}{3}$ is not even close, and $512 = \sqrt{64^{3}}$ is the value of $64^{\frac{3}{2}}$, with the roles of $2$ and $3$ swapped.

questions.stem_md: A game board has $2^{n+3}$ squares at level $n$. This number is equal to

questions.solution_md:
(a) $9^{y} = 3^{2y} = 3^{12}$ gives $y = 6$; $27^{z} = 3^{3z} = 3^{12}$ gives $z = 4$. Also $b^{2} = 81$ and $ac = 3 \times 27 = 81$.

(b) $8^{y} = 2^{3y} = 2^{15}$ gives $y = 5$; $32^{z} = 2^{5z} = 2^{15}$ gives $z = 3$. Then $\dfrac{1}{15} + \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{1 + 5}{15} = \dfrac{2}{5} = \dfrac{2}{y}$.

(b) Rohit writes $(5^{2})^{3} = 5^{5} = 3125$. [3]

(b) The indices should be multiplied: $5^{6} = 15625$.

(a) For a product of powers of the same base, the base stays and the indices add: $2^{5} \times 2^{3} = 2^{8} = 256$. Multiplying the bases ($2 \times 2 = 4$) and adding the indices is wrong: $4^{8} = 65536$.

(b) A power of a power multiplies the indices: $(5^{2})^{3} = 5^{2 \times 3} = 5^{6} = 15625$. Adding the indices gives $5^{5} = 3125$, which is smaller.

(c) For $x = 1$ the left side is $9^{1} = 9$ and the right side is $27^{0} = 1$, so $x = 1$ is wrong. Her mistake: $27^{x-1} = (3^{3})^{x-1} = 3^{3(x-1)} = 3^{3x-3}$; she did not multiply $3$ by both terms of $x - 1$. Correct equation: $2x = 3x - 3$, so $x = 3$.
